If an update to an event is interrupted by another event between the time
the initial event allocated its buffer and where it wrote to the
write_stamp
column2: the code try to reset the write stamp back to the what it had

column1: just overwritten. It knows that it was overwritten via checking the
before_stamp
column2: and if it didn't match what it wrote to the before_stamp

column1: before it allocated its space
To put back the write_stamp
column2: it uses the before_stamp it read. The problem

column1: here is that by writing the before_stamp to the write_stamp it makes the
two equal again
column2: which means that the write_stamp can be considered valid

column1: as the last timestamp written to the ring buffer. But this is not
necessarily true. The event that interrupted the event could have been
interrupted in a way that it was interrupted as well
leaving with an invalid write_stamp. But if this happens and returns to
this context that uses the before_stamp to update the write_stamp again
it can possibly incorrectly make it valid
column2: causing later events to have in

column1: correct time stamps.
As it is OK to leave this function with an invalid write_stamp (one that
doesn't match the before_stamp)
column2: there's no reason to try to make it valid

column1: again in this case. If this race happens
column2: then just leave with the invalid

column1: write_stamp and the next event to come along will just add a absolute
timestamp and validate everything again.
Bonus points: This gets rid of another cmpxchg64!
